solutions.check: 26 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Part of American's address: "Male flasher's rules of conduct"?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the US postal number at the end of an address
second, comic meaning: a man who exposes himself works with his trouser fly, so his code of conduct is a code for the fly

explanation.surface: A quotation lifted from an American's speech, apparently about a code of behaviour for exhibitionists.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and quotation marks flag the second reading as a joke: split the answer into a trouser fastener plus a set of rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans write this five-digit postal number at the end of a mailing address, the equivalent of a British postcode.

clue.text: Toady's row about distribution of loot

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the quarrel word goes round the other letters

parts.note: to row is to squabble or bicker

indicators.note: distributing things spreads them about, so the following word is shared out into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A crook's sycophant argues over how the stolen goods are to be divided up.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', so the clue says the toady IS the wordplay; BICKER opens after its B to take the shuffled loot.
explanation.definitionFit: A toady is a fawning flatterer, and a bootlicker is the same servile sycophant in blunter slang.

clue.text: Bureaucrat here in Strasbourg buried in beastly waste

indicators.note: something buried lies inside something else, so the first piece goes within the second

parts.note: offal is the entrails and waste parts of a slaughtered animal
ici is French for here, and Strasbourg is in France

explanation.surface: A dig at a European Parliament functionary in Strasbourg drowning in bestial rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: An official is a person holding a public office, especially a functionary in a government department, which is what a bureaucrat is.

clue.text: Idiot swallowing up drugs should be locked up

indicators.note: whatever swallows something holds it inside, so the idiot word wraps round the rest

parts.note: a clod is a dull, stupid person

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the drug letters are read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: E is ecstasy, so drugs are Es

explanation.surface: A fool who gulps down pills ought to be put behind bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Something closed has been shut and secured, the same state as being locked up.

clue.text: (& 22ac./18ac.) Frottage exponent's trousers quicker than average to show this?

definitions.text: Frottage exponent's trousers quicker than average to show this?

parts.words: Frottage exponent's trousers quicker than average to show this?
parts.note: surface reading: what tell-tale sign do the trousers of someone who gets off by rubbing against strangers display?

parts.words: Frottage exponent's trousers quicker than average to show this?
parts.note: setter's reading: constant friction damages cloth, so the stock phrase for the deterioration of everyday use is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Frottage is sexual rubbing against others, often in crowds; the joke is that such friction would simply age the cloth faster.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the gradual damage that everyday use and friction cause to clothes and other things.

clue.text: Crow hogs X-Factor finale — hiss!

indicators.note: to hog something is to keep it all to yourself, so the crowing word holds the other letter

parts.note: to crow is to laugh triumphantly, to cackle

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so only the end letter of the TV show's name is taken

parts.note: the TV talent show's name ends in R

explanation.surface: Someone gloats over the end of the talent show, prompting boos and hissing.
explanation.walkthrough: The X Factor was a British TV singing contest. The dash makes 'hiss' look like a heckle; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Crackle and hiss are both the sharp static noises of a poor radio signal or old record.

clue.text: Leads applying electric current to head of penis (swells on the outside)

indicators.note: being on the outside means wrapping round, so the posh people word surrounds the other pair

parts.note: swells and toffs are both old slang for upper-class dandies
I is the physics symbol for current

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the start of the next word counts

parts.note: the initial of penis

explanation.surface: Sounds like grim instructions about wiring electrodes to a man's genitals, with swelling noted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leads' means clues for an investigator, not wires; current plus the P sit together inside the posh-people word, after its T.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip-off is a piece of inside information, just as police follow leads given by informants.

clue.text: In which 'X' and 'Y' often appear shaking a leg, putting on underwear

indicators.note: shaking jumbles things up, so the letters of the following words fall into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these two words rearranged
a bra is an item of underwear

explanation.surface: A striptease in reverse: someone wiggles a leg while dressing in lingerie, with X and Y nowhere explained.
explanation.definitionFit: Algebra is the branch of maths in which letters such as x and y stand for unknown numbers.

clue.text: see 21dn.
Hot revered Royal's divine talent — for being caught out in a scandal?

definitions.text: being caught out in a scandal

parts.note: hot and in both mean fashionable
Di is Princess Diana, the revered royal; the 's stays
grace is a gift bestowed by God

explanation.surface: A gushing tabloid line about a royal's heaven-sent gifts, then a dash hinting at scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Princess Diana was widely called Di; the possessive 's is kept as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone exposed in a scandal has fallen out of favour, which is what being in disgrace means.

clue.text: Scarper when party errand boy grabs one

indicators.note: grabbing something takes hold of it, so the party and errand boy pair clasp the number between them

parts.note: a do is a party
a means one
a runner carries messages and runs errands

explanation.surface: Time to flee when the party's messenger lad snatches something.
explanation.walkthrough: The party and the errand boy together form the container, with the one held at their join.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarper and do a runner are both British slang for running away, especially to avoid paying.

clue.text: Successful candidate's dim denial about "admitting brother's number one"

indicators.note: admitting someone lets them in, so the rearranged phrase takes the letter inside
about means all around, so the phrase it follows is turned round into a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters of these two words, to be rearranged

indicators.note: number one means the first, so only the initial of the sibling word is taken

parts.note: the initial of brother

explanation.surface: A stupid denial by the winner that a brother was first choice.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Miliband beat his brother David to the Labour leadership in 2010, so the surface's sibling rivalry is the real story.
explanation.definitionFit: Ed Miliband won the 2010 Labour leadership contest, making him the victorious contender.

clue.text: Female Cyclops is going to stuff

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female
the setter, Cyclops, would say I'll, meaning I will

explanation.surface: A woman setter announcing she is about to stuff something.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by their pseudonym; Cyclops is going = I'll, apostrophe dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill something is to stuff it full, as with a cushion or a turkey.

clue.text: Indicate warning of course against what Labour's top guns are now?

parts.note: golfers shout fore to warn people on the course

parts.words: what Labour's top guns are now
parts.note: out of power, Labour's senior figures form the shadow cabinet

explanation.surface: A political jibe that Labour's big beasts are now only fit to signal warnings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally'; it is the golf course. In Britain the opposition's front bench is called the shadow cabinet.
explanation.definitionFit: To foreshadow is to give an early hint or sign of something to come, to indicate it in advance.

clue.text: Shenanigans of unstable Labour heads with stupid grudge, collared by broadcaster

indicators.note: a collar goes round the neck, so the broadcaster's name encircles everything else

parts.note: Sky is a British satellite TV broadcaster

indicators.note: heads are the leading letters, so the first letters of the two preceding words are taken

parts.note: the first letters of these two words

indicators.note: something stupid is senseless and muddled, so the letters of the next word are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Political TV news on wobbly Labour leaders nursing a petty grudge, cornered by a broadcaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unstable' looks like the anagram signal, but it only supplies its initial; 'stupid' is what scrambles the grudge.
explanation.definitionFit: Skulduggery is underhand scheming and trickery, much the same as shenanigans.

clue.text: Labour's leader into teasing crushed Balls and the like

indicators.note: going into something puts it inside, so the single letter is placed within the other letters
something crushed is broken out of its shape, so the letters of the word teasing are reformed

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: the leader is whoever goes first, so the first letter of the party name is taken

parts.note: the initial of Labour

explanation.surface: Labour's leader goading a beaten Ed Balls and colleagues, Balls being a Labour politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was a senior Labour shadow minister, so 'Balls' reads as a name; here it is the anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Balls is slang for testicles, which are examples of the sexual organs called genitals.

clue.text: Journalist turned over by criminal plea in court

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the journalist letters run backwards

parts.note: ED is short for editor, the standard crossword journalist
a fence is a criminal who handles stolen goods

explanation.surface: A reporter is beaten by a crook's argument in the courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like an anagram signal; here it is a noun for a dealer in stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A defence is the case or plea an accused person puts forward in court to answer a charge.

clue.text: Rambler's turn with slut

parts.note: to wind is to turn, as a road or a key does
bag is a derogatory slang word for a woman

explanation.surface: A hiker takes his turn walking alongside a loose woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rambler' suggests a hiker; the definition means someone who rambles on in speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A windbag talks at tedious length, exactly what a verbal rambler does.

clue.text: see 5dn.
Fruity thing could have you on your back in no time

definitions.text: Fruity thing could have you on your back in no time

parts.words: Fruity thing could have you on your back in no time
parts.note: surface reading: something racy or saucy that could get you into bed very fast

parts.words: Fruity thing could have you on your back in no time
parts.note: setter's reading: a literal piece of fruit peel that makes you slip and fall flat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruity' in British slang means sexually suggestive, steering towards seduction; the clue really wants the slapstick peel.
explanation.definitionFit: The peel of this yellow fruit is the classic slippery cause of a comic fall, and figuratively any embarrassing blunder.

clue.text: Mark Thatcher's first love under the table

parts.note: a blot is a mark or stain

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter only of the surname before it

parts.note: the initial of Thatcher
love is zero in tennis scoring, the letter O

explanation.surface: Mark Thatcher, Margaret Thatcher's son, and his first love ending up drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark Thatcher' reads as one person, the former PM's son; split it into a stain plus a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Blotto is slang for extremely drunk, and someone under the table has drunk until collapsing.

clue.text: Government expert re-engineered crotch — neat!

indicators.note: re-engineering something rebuilds it differently, so the following letters are reassembled

parts.note: the letters of these two words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A boffin admiring an apparently neat bit of surgical rebuilding down below.
explanation.definitionFit: A technocrat is a technical specialist given power in government, an expert running the state.

clue.text: (& 9ac.) Small glass of beer dropped when pissed

parts.note: in a British pub a half is half a pint
to cut something, such as a scene, is to drop it

explanation.surface: A drunk lets a small beer slip from his hand.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang pissed means drunk, not angry as in America.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-cut is British slang for fairly drunk, and pissed is the cruder word for the same state.

clue.text: see5dn.
Bill, nothing on, Lewinsky initially agitated, yet a devoted follower

indicators.note: agitated means stirred up, so the following short word is jumbled

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
nothing is zero, the letter O

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of the surname is used

parts.note: the initial of Lewinsky
the letters of yet rearranged

explanation.surface: Bill Clinton with nothing on and Monica Lewinsky flustered, yet she was a devoted follower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' with Lewinsky suggests Clinton; it is an account. Nothing is placed on, that is after, the bill.
explanation.definitionFit: An acolyte is an assistant or loyal follower, originally an altar attendant in church.

clue.text: Beaten Gore really tried to be President?

definitions.note: an adjective defining a noun: an also-ran is someone beaten

parts.note: Al Gore, the US vice-president who lost the 2000 presidential election
so and really both mean very
to run for office is to stand as a candidate

explanation.surface: A wistful note on Al Gore, who truly tried for the White House and lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gore' is a first name hunt: the surname gives his forename AL.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a loser in a race or election, someone beaten into the unplaced field.
